title: Half the register, 51.7%, lives where he has never held office
question: Where does the electorate sit, and where has he held office?
takeaway: The 275,570-voter pool in Mwingi and Kitui South is the ground the nomination is won or lost on; Kitui Central, which he has represented since 2013, is 14.6% of the register.

title: The proposal runs evidence first: what Kitui is and needs, the contest, the strategy, the plan, how it is proven and kept lawful, and the decision
question: What is the shape of the argument?
takeaway: Kitui today and The contest are the evidence; The strategy and The plan are built on it; Proof and protection shows how it is measured and kept safe; The decision closes with what Dr. Mulu is asked to decide. The evidence behind it follows, then the working platform.

title: There are about eleven months to the election, and the nomination window comes first, within weeks
question: How long is there?
takeaway: The Wiper ticket is settled in a window reported for late October to November 2026; everything the engagement does before then is aimed at it.

title: Each of the five objectives answers one finding and is judged by one observable measure
question: What are the five objectives, and what does each serve?
takeaway: No objective stands on its own: each starts from a finding in Section 2 and ends in an indicator in Section 18.1.

title: His team analyses, sets the strategy and directs on the platform, and keeps publishing throughout
question: How does the work run?
takeaway: Firefly publishes nothing on his accounts and operates no channel: it runs the platform the team works on.

title: Every measure of success is observable on his channels or the SMS list, and each baseline is set in Week 1
question: How will success be judged?
takeaway: The scorecard starts empty by design: the Week 1 export sets each baseline from his own channels and the SMS list.

title: The register grew by 72,945 voters since 2022, most of them in one thirty-day drive
question: How big is the register, and how did it get there?
takeaway: Kitui has 605,703 registered voters as of July 2026; the 2022 split by constituency is the latest published, because the 2026 register is not yet out by ward.

title: Every countywide seat in 2022 was won with about 200,000 votes, and one winner beat the governor's total
question: What does it take to win a countywide seat in Kitui?
takeaway: The 198,004 line is the working bar: the Woman Representative cleared it, the Senator came within 6,687, and both are Wiper rivals for the ticket.

title: The nomination method is reported, not confirmed, and two documents would settle it
question: What is the nomination method, and how confident are we?
takeaway: Until the party's resolution or its 2027 nomination rules are in hand, every phase that leans on the reported selection method is a plan against a Tier 3 report.

title: Kitui is 95.2% rural, and more than half its residents are poor
question: Who lives in Kitui?
takeaway: A county of 1,136,187 people across 30,430 km², with livestock at the centre of its economy, and at Alert Phase in the NDMA's January 2026 drought bulletin.

title: The next governor runs a KSh 13.79bn envelope, and 84.3% of it arrives from the national government
question: What does the next governor actually control?
takeaway: Own-source revenue is the one part the county raises itself: KSh 1.12bn in the Fiscal Strategy Paper, KSh 1.339bn after the Assembly's revision, until the final approved budget settles it.

title: Internet use nearly doubled since 2019, while phone ownership barely moved
question: How do people get online, and has that changed?
takeaway: Even after the rise, 73.8% of Kitui is offline, and fewer than half of residents own a phone.

title: Three of the Kikamba stations are tied to political figures, so placement goes to the independents
question: Who owns the airwaves, and where do we place vs monitor?
takeaway: Musyi, County FM and Wikwatyo carry the campaign's placements; the Ngilu-linked stations and the party leader's station are watched, not relied on.

title: Thirteen years as MP have left a checkable record: 12,573 bursaries and the best-evaluated constituency in the Eastern region
question: What has he actually done?
takeaway: His distinguishing proof is delivery on the record, and most of it is already published on the constituency's own NG-CDF site.

title: His presence is one Facebook page, a quiet X account and a constituency site that already holds his record
question: What does his presence look like against the field?
takeaway: The NG-CDF site is the most under-used asset here; the comparison with the field is drawn in the Week 1 audit.

title: To win, he needs about 60.8% of the ballots cast, on the 2022 register
question: What is the winning number?
takeaway: 200,000 votes is the 2022 winner's total rounded; the same share of the larger July 2026 register is ≈225,000.

title: The twelve largest wards hold 37.78% of the register, and half the wards hold 59.13%
question: Where are the votes?
takeaway: Registration is concentrated: the ten smallest wards together hold only 18.10% of voters, across some of the county's widest ground.

title: No route clears 200,000 on its own ballots, and the home belt falls furthest short
question: Which route to the number is real, and which is a trap?
takeaway: Even every ballot in the home belt leaves him 81,653 short: a route is where the margin is built, and Mwingi is part of any route that works.

title: 51.7% of the register lives in the four constituencies where he has never held office
question: Where has he held office, and what does that leave untouched?
takeaway: The 275,570-voter pool is structural, derived from where he has held office, not from any measure of opinion; 5 of the twelve largest wards are in it.

title: Four of the field have already won a countywide race, and he has not yet stood for one
question: What has each contender already proven at the ballot?
takeaway: Kasalu's 201,899 beat the winning governor's total; his own proof at the ballot is constituency-bounded.

title: Two constituencies with 26.4% of the register returned non-Wiper MPs, and his own seat has its own race
question: Where will party loyalty not carry him?
takeaway: Kitui East and Kitui South are a direct-contact problem, not a party-mobilisation one, and Kitui Central cannot be left on autopilot.

title: The three zones hold 78.8% of residents, and Kitui Rural falls in none of them
question: How do the three zones differ, and who is left out?
takeaway: About 240,000 residents and 10.3% of the register sit outside the zoning; Kitui Rural needs a zone or a stated reason it is out.

title: Digital reaches at most 158,696 voters, 41,304 short of the benchmark before a single one is persuaded
question: What can digital physically reach?
takeaway: 447,007 registered voters are not reachable online: SMS, USSD, radio and the ground carry the rest.

title: His profile carries six errors a researcher would find in an afternoon, and the Week 1 audit reads the rest
question: What does his current presence actually show?
takeaway: The six fixes are Section 14.3; the four audit figures are drawn from the Week 1 export, never from an estimate.

title: 6 things no published source can tell the analysis, and none is estimated
question: What can't the data tell us yet, and what closes each gap?
takeaway: The analysis works from where he has held office and from certified totals, not from ward-level preference or ward returns no one has published.

title: The diagnosis is a recognition gap outside Kitui Central, and one rival's result is the strongest evidence against it
question: How strong is the diagnosis, and what would overturn it?
takeaway: Week 1 tests it against his own channel data before anything is committed: if his reach already lands in Mwingi, the problem is message, not reach.

title: Township carries the most itemised spend placed on one ward, KSh 115.9m across 27 projects
question: Where does the scorecard place its itemised projects, ward by ward, against how many voters each ward holds?
takeaway: 339 of the 401 itemised projects name one ward and are drawn on it; the other 62 are totalled apart, never spread across wards.

title: One position, three pillars that argue it, and a record that holds it up
question: What is the position, and what holds it up?
takeaway: Every message rests on something already on the public record; none rests on a promise alone.

title: In the Nomination sprint, 65% of the effort goes to Mwingi and the arid belt, well above their share of residents
question: Where does the effort go in the Nomination sprint?
takeaway: The weighting over-indexes on the pool on the working hypothesis that his gap there is one of recognition; 65% of digital reach effort is geofenced to it.

title: Six segments, three sized in voters from the census and three with context but no published voter count
question: Who are we trying to move, and how much do they matter?
takeaway: Sizes overlap and are not additive; where no source publishes a voter count, none is given.

title: Each region hears a different case for the same candidate, and Kikamba travels by voice, never by bulk SMS
question: What do we say where, and in which language?
takeaway: The anchor hears his record, Mwingi hears a published allocation method, the arid belt hears infrastructure; the language follows the channel.

title: The same seven days become six briefed posts across four content types, and Thursday's commitment returns as a Sunday check
question: What gets published, and when?
takeaway: Two fields on a Thursday post and a language rule change the week; who takes the photograph and who presses publish do not.

title: Radio's share of effort nearly doubles and digital's falls to 18%, because digital cannot reach the number
question: How does effort move between channels?
takeaway: 82% of effort goes offline; radio placement goes only to the stations Section 4.2 marks for placement.

title: Six profile corrections, each minutes of work, and the missing PhD comes first
question: What gets fixed first?
takeaway: The doctorate is the differentiator no rival holds, and it is absent from the one field a voter checks.

title: Seven findings the Week 1 audit could return, each with the change it triggers, fixed in advance
question: When does the plan change?
takeaway: Stating the rules before the audit means the data cannot be read backwards into whatever was already planned.

title: Fourteen workstreams in four groups: your team runs them on Firefly's platform, and keeps publishing
question: What does each group produce, and who owns each workstream?
takeaway: Most of the output is your team's existing work, now directed by the team itself; Firefly's own product is the platform. Workstream 9, the offline layer, is the one the race turns on; two workstreams sit outside the operation.

title: The first week measures, and nothing is committed against the diagnosis until it has
question: What happens in the first four weeks?
takeaway: Week 1 is the audit; the brief starts in Week 2, weighted to the pool, and the six fixes ship by the end of it.

title: Five phases run to the election; the Nomination sprint runs ahead of the Wiper decision, not with it
question: How does the plan run to August 2027?
takeaway: The Nomination sprint is the team's work period, weeks 1–6 from signature; Wiper's decision is a separate window, reported for late October to November 2026. Three general-election phases keep their calendar dates to 10 August 2027.

title: Three indicators climb through every phase, and every other target belongs to one phase
question: What does each phase have to deliver?
takeaway: Consented SMS contacts rise from 40,000 in the Awareness phase to 120,000 by the Turnout phase; rows marked ° are operational diagnostics, not performance indicators.

title: He receives a brief every week and a read every month, and the level sets how deep each goes
question: What does he receive, and how often?
takeaway: Standard, the recommended level, is the one at which all 40 wards carry reach reporting and an active SMS and USSD layer.

title: Nine indicators judge the work, four for the nomination and five for the election, each observable on his own channels or lists
question: How is progress measured?
takeaway: Every indicator is observable on his channels, the SMS list or the field record, and each stays empty until its baseline is taken.

title: Your team drafts and publishes, one named counterpart approves, and an attack is judged against four severity tiers
question: How are decisions made?
takeaway: Your strategy core approves new claims and Kikamba output, your team publishes everything, the offline broadcasts included, and Firefly publishes nothing; a critical attack reaches the candidate, with the war room convened within fifteen minutes.

title: Two of the six risks would change the plan rather than damage it, and both are settled by measurement early
question: What could go wrong?
takeaway: R1 closes with the party's 2027 nomination rules, R2 with the Week 1 audit. The incumbent is term-limited under Article 180(7), so the plan is for an open seat.

title: The campaign names three strategy roles and removes no one, with five surge roles each tied to a trigger; Firefly runs the platform
question: What shape is the team?
takeaway: The campaign's command structure and his publishing team stay as they are; the strategy director reports to one named counterpart and briefs one named lead.

title: Every report ends in a published outcome, and the reporter hears back twice
question: What happens to a report in the service-delivery tracker?
takeaway: The register shows what was reported, what was raised and what happened, failures included.

title: The doorstep and the ad audience update each other within a day
question: How do the field and digital operations learn from each other?
takeaway: The opt-in rate on routed doors keeps both sides honest: if routed doors do no better than the rest, the routing is wrong.

title: Six options on any phone, and the third puts the tracker in reach of a feature phone in Mutha
question: What does the USSD menu offer?
takeaway: Dial the shortcode, read the plan, register, report an issue, volunteer or opt in, with no internet and close to no cost.

title: Five components, and the personal data concentrates in the first two
question: What does each component of the stack do, hold and risk?
takeaway: The gateway and the CRM carry the high and critical data-protection exposure; the other three work on public or anonymised data, and every one awaits a campaign decision.

title: The campaign provides 9 things, and three of them gate everything else
question: What does the campaign provide?
takeaway: A counterpart, read-only access and the data-protection reviewer come first; the rest follow once the engagement is running.

title: The ask is one decision, to approve the platform, because the nomination window sets the clock
question: What is being asked?
takeaway: Each week of delay is a week less of directed output before a window reported for late October; the 275,570-voter pool is where that output goes.

title: Six ways of cutting the same electorate, and two of them decide the channel plan
question: This proposal's Kitui County audience architecture overview
takeaway: Connectivity and language are the two facets the rest of the proposal turns on: 73.8% offline sets the channel mix, ~76% Kikamba sets the language mix. The 73.8% / 26.2% split is the CA/KNBS 2023/24 rate, which supersedes the 2019 census's 86.4% / 13.6%.

title: Every visit logs a commitment, and twelve weeks later the tracker says what happened to it
question: The visit-to-verification loop
takeaway: It is a loop: the verification publishes to the tracker whether the commitment was kept or not, and that record is what the next visit is measured against. “Published either way” is the block's own phrase and the whole of its argument.

title: Three things every figure in this document has to carry
question: The tri-partite provenance mandate
takeaway: Source, date and geographic unit. Every figure in this pass carries all three in its “View the data” disclosure, which is the document's own rule applied to the document's own charts.

title: Three tiers, and only one of them may move money
question: The three-tier evidential classification — tier, source types, authorised strategic use
takeaway: The authorised-use column is what makes the tiers operational rather than descriptive: Tier 3 is strictly prohibited from driving financial or resource reallocation without escalation. Every figure in this pass carries the tier the section states, and flags disagreement rather than resolving it — which is C-8 and C-9.

title: What to do when two sources disagree, in four steps the document wrote for itself
question: The conflict resolution protocol, in order
takeaway: Step 4 is the one this audit has been applying throughout: where the document disagrees with itself, both numbers are shown with their sources and neither is averaged away. The steps are numbered because they are tried in order — the methodological audit only applies once the tier test comes back equal.

title: Six segments, six messages, and a named evidence source behind every one
question: The message-by-demographic-segment matrix — segment, tailored message and Kikamba framing, verifiable evidence
takeaway: The evidence column is not decoration: the approval gateway makes a primary citation mandatory at drafting, and this matrix is where each segment's citation is named. The Kikamba framings are transcribed exactly, diacritics included.

title: Five channels, each with its own register and its own proof
question: The message-by-channel matrix — channel and reach, format and linguistic style, evidential proof points
takeaway: Reach is shown only where a source supports it: the SMS layer (phone owners not online) and the online audience, both read from the registry. Radio, caravans and church have no measured reach in Kitui. The channels overlap and must not be added.

title: Three decision levels, three authorities, and the candidate is only in the last
question: The operational escalation path — issues, resolution authority and the rule at each decision level. Attacks on the campaign are judged separately, by the severity tiers in Risks & response
takeaway: The levels are numbered because escalation is ordered: a level 1 issue that is not resolved inside the hour becomes a level 2 issue, and the authority changes with it. Each level names who decides and what they must do, which is what makes it a protocol rather than a list.

title: Four severity tiers, and the first instruction is to do nothing
question: The response decision tree: severity tier, threshold, protocol, turnaround and who approves
takeaway: Level 1's protocol is IGNORE / PASSIVE MONITOR, with an explicit instruction not to amplify or refute. It is the most easily lost line in the runbook and the one that decides whether a fringe post stays fringe. The thresholds are stated in advance, which is what makes the matrix usable at speed.

title: From fifteen minutes on air to twenty-four hours in print
question: The rapid response SLA by channel
takeaway: The ladder runs from the fastest channel to the slowest, which is also the order a rebuttal travels: radio first, then WhatsApp, then digital, then print. Bulk SMS is not on the clock: the 48-hour lodging rule in Ground & offline rules it out of rapid response.

title: Four attack lines, four answers, and two sources that say the answer is not ready yet
question: The pre-drafted holding positions — attack line, holding message, Kikamba framing and primary source
takeaway: TWO OF THE FOUR SOURCE CELLS DECLINE TO CLAIM SOMETHING, and both are kept exactly. Position 1 says the classroom and bursary counts are pending the inventory and that only the record's 12,573 recipients and KSh 47m should be used until reconciled. Position 2 says the ward allocation methodology does not exist yet and the line should not go on air before it does. A runbook that hid either would be a runbook that sends a spokesperson on air with an unverified figure.

title: Three statutes, and a signature count worked to its stricter reading
question: The statutory compliance architecture
takeaway: The endorsement count was stated two ways, 500 per sub-county (4,000) or 500 from at least 5 of the 8 (500 in total). A paper short of the statutory count is rejected and a surplus is not, so the campaign works to 4,000; the statutory figure is confirmed with counsel before filing.

title: Seven clearances at five different stages, and one the campaign will not yet claim
question: This proposal's IEBC statutory nomination clearance checklist — dimension, statutory standard, current status
takeaway: The status column is the point: two Verified, one Active, one Scheduled, one Pending the filing window, one Operationalized — and one that reads “[Requires legal confirmation]”, the document declining to claim a deadline it has not confirmed.

title: Three exposures, and two of them end in a custodial sentence
question: This proposal's DPA 2019 and Election Offences statutory matrix — obligation, exposure, mitigation
takeaway: The exposure column carries the penalty as the document states it — Ksh 5,000,000 or two years, and disqualification plus five years — because a mitigation protocol read without its exposure is a procedure rather than a reason.

title: A lean core of three leads, each directing subcontracted specialists
question: The lean core plus specialist vendor model
takeaway: The three leads report to the Campaign Manager and the specialists are subcontracted, not hired. No role or headcount has been added: this is exactly the set the block named.

title: Four core roles, and every specialist in the campaign reports through one of them
question: The core campaign roles and ownership matrix — role, ownership, subcontractors directed
takeaway: No role, headcount or vendor has been added. The SMS/USSD gateway vendor is stated as “selected at contracting”, which is the same pending state the procurement matrix records for every one of its five rows.

title: Two teams, one weekly brief, and a single named counterpart between them and the candidate
question: The reporting lines
takeaway: The weekly brief is the join: the publishing team and the strategy core meet there, and one named counterpart carries it upward. Firefly runs the platform beneath both.

title: One programme tests whether the deficit is real; the other is the evidence it argues with
question: The tests of the recognition hypothesis, and the service-delivery tracker
takeaway: The research programme feeds the tracker: what the audit establishes about a ward becomes a baseline the tracker publishes against. 19B is stated as a dual asset — campaign evidence now, and a governing dashboard from day one.

title: Three instruments, and each one names the decision it unlocks
question: The tests of the recognition-deficit hypothesis — module, method, record, timing and the decision it unlocks
takeaway: The last column is what makes this a decision instrument: the audit's result routes directly to a stated change of plan, set out in advance in this proposal. All three read records that already exist: his own analytics, the IEBC's published forms and the line his team operates.

title: Four delivery dimensions, two of which are still waiting on a ledger
question: The public service-delivery tracker — dimension, statutory sources, update cadence and verification
takeaway: The classroom and TVET counts and the bursary receipt count are stated as pending the project ledger, and they are printed that way rather than filled with an estimate. The record's 12,573 bursary recipients is the Tier 1 figure the document does have, and the row says so.

title: Four content types feed two engines, and everything leaves through one gateway
question: This proposal's 360° content production pipeline
takeaway: The gateway is the point of the diagram: both engines converge on it, so no asset reaches a voter without the four-step sign-off this proposal specifies. Nothing routes around it.

title: Five channels, and only one of them may carry Kikamba text
question: The production format specifications — channel, technical specification, language and creative treatment
takeaway: The SMS row states the constraint twice over: “Kiswahili or English only (CA rule)”, and GSM-7 encoding with no accented unicode — which rules out the ĩ and ũ Kikamba orthography needs. Kikamba travels by radio, voice notes and USSD instead.

title: Approval falls on Wednesday, which is what makes Friday's market broadcast possible
question: The weekly 7-day content production cycle — focus and output deliverables per day
takeaway: The week is built backwards from Friday's markets: scripts Monday, studio Tuesday, the approval gateway Wednesday, print and radio dispatch Thursday. Friday's row states 100,000 ward SMS delivered, which this proposal's KPI ladder is the place to check against.

title: Nothing reaches a voter without a citation at the front and a logged signature at the end
question: The four-step content approval gateway, in order
takeaway: Numbered because the order is the control: a citation attached at step 1 is what steps 2 and 3 have to check, and the audit register entry at step 4 is what makes the whole chain reviewable afterwards.

title: Seven vaults, and the second one holds the evidence every asset has to cite
question: The campaign asset repository
takeaway: 02_PRIMARY_EVIDENCE_VAULT is the one that makes the approval gateway's first step workable: the OAG certificates, the Hansard records and the KNBS baselines a drafter must attach a citation from are filed in one place rather than looked up each time.

title: What a ward coordinator hears at 18:00 can be answered on air the next morning
question: The closed-loop field and digital integration engine
takeaway: It is a loop, not a funnel: the inbound pipeline feeds the war room, the war room feeds the outbound pipeline and the physical channels, and what those produce comes back as field intelligence. The ASCII drew that with arrows; the order and this line carry it instead.

title: Four report types, one of which has a thirty-minute clock on it
question: The ward coordinator field reporting protocol — type, frequency, channel and fields captured
takeaway: The Critical Threat Flash is the only one with a deadline measured in minutes, and the only one routed to a direct phone rather than a queue. The other three are daily, weekly and weekly, and every one names the fields it captures.

title: A rumour logged by USSD is answered in three languages across four channels inside four hours
question: The ground-to-digital cycle, on the clock
takeaway: The clock is the claim, so it runs down the margin rather than sitting in a caption. The SMS step goes to the consented voters in Tseikuru and Kyuso, from a message lodged 48 hours ahead; how large that list is, is the target ladder's to answer, not this figure's.

title: Seven standing forums, and the candidate is named in three of them
question: The campaign operational rhythm and governance cadence — time, forum, agenda, owner and participants
takeaway: The cadence is repeated on every row rather than merged down a column. A merged cell is a thing a screen reader reads once and a stacked phone layout loses entirely, and the cost of repeating it is two words.

title: Everything captured is tagged, consented and tiered before it reaches a channel
question: The campaign data layer architecture — capture, validation, output, and the core beneath them
takeaway: The ASCII original joined these with arrows. Arrows are the part that cannot survive a reflow, so the order carries the flow and the line above says in words what the arrows said: capture feeds validation, validation feeds the channels, and everything passes through the encrypted core.

title: Nineteen fields, four of them about consent and one that can never be reversed
question: The supporter record schema — field, type, and the constraint on each
takeaway: Transcribed field for field, including the enum members and their order: msisdn_hash is a one-way SHA-256 identifier and phone_encrypted is reversible AES-256-GCM for authorised SMS, and those are not interchangeable. It is now a real table — searchable, readable in order by a screen reader, and wrapping rather than scrolling sideways on a phone.

title: Six sections of the Data Protection Act 2019, and what each one obliges the campaign to build
question: The statutory compliance checklist — the legal requirement against the operational implementation
takeaway: Each requirement cites its section of the Act. The pairing is the content, so each is drawn as one card rather than two columns that could shear apart at a narrow width.

title: Four tiers, and the personal data lives in exactly one of them
question: The campaign technology stack architecture
takeaway: Tier 1 collects the phone numbers and tier 2 holds them encrypted; tiers 3 and 4 work on public and anonymised data. The procurement matrix rates the DPA risk of each accordingly, and every one of its five rows is still awaiting a campaign decision.

title: Five components, rated for data-protection risk, and not one of them decided
question: The technology stack master procurement matrix
takeaway: All five rows read “Awaiting campaign decision” in the source and all five read it here. A figure that rendered a pending procurement as settled would be inventing the most consequential kind of thing in this chapter.

title: Four ways to reach 532,758 voters without a commercial gatekeeper's permission
question: The gatekeeper bypass and direct reach architecture: the operational protocol for each route
takeaway: Four routes run in parallel but are stood up in order. Mang'elete, named in the first route, is in no ownership map; the ownership map in Who owns the airwaves governs.

title: Three ground rumours, and the evidence the campaign answers each with
question: The rumour-and-rebuttal protocol, paired
takeaway: One of the three rebuttals ends “Share pending the ledger” — the document declining to claim a proportion it has not verified, inside its own counter-messaging table. It is kept exactly.

title: Four terms where the literal translation loses the argument
question: The proverbial framing protocol — the term, the translation that fails, and the approved idiom
takeaway: Every Kikamba string is transcribed with its diacritics exactly as this proposal prints them. ĩ and ũ are distinct letters rather than decorated vowels, and this proposal's own rules of engagement forbid machine translation of Kikamba for this reason.

title: Four gates between an English draft and a Kikamba broadcast
question: The translation and quality-control gateway, in order
takeaway: Numbered because it is a real sequence: the reverse-translation audit cannot run before the adaptation it audits exists, and the cultural sign-off is the last gate before release.

title: Three languages, and three quarters of the county reachable in only one of them
question: Estimated primary reach per language, as this proposal states it
takeaway: The three shares are stated in this proposal without a citation and sum to 100%, so they describe who speaks what (a language map, unconfirmed), not a target. The content target is the 50 / 30 / 20 mix in this proposal; bulk SMS carries Kiswahili and English only.

title: Every medium is allocated to the whole, and only one of them is allocated to Kikamba alone
question: The language allocation per campaign output medium. Each row totals 100%.
takeaway: The bulk SMS row gives Kikamba no allocation, as the bulk SMS rule requires: the Communications Authority restricts political bulk SMS to English or Kiswahili. USSD is not restricted, and takes 50% Kikamba here.

title: Four of the eight constituencies hold 296,196 voters, 55.60% of the county, across 22 wards
question: Registered voters per constituency, largest first, with ward count and average ward size
takeaway: The "Big 4" (Kitui Central, Kitui South, Mwingi Central, Mwingi North) are where the register is; read with the ward map, they are where the effort is weighed.
